title: Matter Is Made of Particles
seo_title: Grade 5 Matter and Particles Worksheets: Solids, Liquids, Gases and Particle Models
standard_text: Develop a model to describe that matter is made of particles too small to be seen.
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 science worksheets on matter and particles (NGSS 5-PS1-1): what matter is, particle models of solids, liquids and gases, and evidence such as air in a syringe and dissolved sugar. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: All matter is made of particles too small to see.
key_sub: Matter has mass and takes up space. In solids the particles are packed in place, in liquids they slide past each other, and in gases they are far apart.
body_html:
How to think about it

Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Rocks, water and air are all matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

All matter is made of particles that are much too small to see. The particles are always moving. How close they are and how they move tells you the state of matter.

You can find evidence for particles you cannot see: air makes a ball firm and can be squeezed in a syringe, dissolved sugar still makes water sweet and heavier, and salt is left behind when salt water evaporates.

Example

A flat ball has a mass of 410 g. After it is pumped full of air its mass is 425 g. What does this show?

425 − 410 = 15 g.

The air pumped in has a mass of 15 g, so air is matter even though you cannot see it.

Answer: Air has mass: 15 g of air.

Example

Sugar is stirred into water until you cannot see it. Is the sugar gone?

The water tastes sweet.

If the water evaporates, sugar is left behind.

The sugar broke into particles too small to see.

Answer: No. It is still there as tiny particles.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air is nothing. Air is matter: it has mass and takes up space.
  • Thinking dissolved sugar or salt is destroyed. It is still there as tiny particles.
  • Thinking particles get bigger when a gas spreads out. The particles stay the same size; the space between them grows.
  • Calling light, heat or sound matter. They are forms of energy, not matter.

faq.a: All matter is made of tiny particles that are much too small to see. Rocks, water and air are all made of particles.
Yes. Air has mass and takes up space. A ball pumped full of air has more mass than the same ball when it is flat.

faq.q: How are particles arranged in solids, liquids and gases?
faq.a: In a solid they are packed in a pattern and vibrate in place. In a liquid they touch but slide past each other. In a gas they are far apart and move freely.

faq.q: What happens to sugar when it dissolves in water?
faq.a: It breaks into particles too small to see that spread through the water. It is still there: the water tastes sweet and its mass goes up by the mass of the sugar.

items.q: Which state of matter takes the shape of its container but keeps the same volume?
items.e: A liquid flows to fit its container, but 1 cup of water is still 1 cup in any glass.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Air has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which tool would help you show that air takes up space?
items.e: As you blow air into a balloon, the balloon gets bigger. The air takes up space inside it.

items.q: What is all matter made of?
c: pieces you can see with your eyes
items.e: All matter is made of particles that are far too small to see, even with a hand lens.

items.q: Which statement about particles is true?
c: Particles are big enough to see with a hand lens.
Particles in a solid never move.
Particles of matter are always moving.
Only gases are made of particles.
items.e: Particles are always moving. In a solid they vibrate in place, in a liquid they slide past each other, and in a gas they move freely.

items.q: Why can't you see the particles that make up a rock?
c: Only liquids are made of particles.
They are much too small to see.
The particles are hidden inside a shell.
items.e: Rocks, water and air are all made of particles. The particles are too small to see.

items.q: Which state of matter spreads out to fill any container?
items.e: Gas particles move freely, so a gas fills the whole container it is in.

items.q: Air is a mixture of gases. Is air matter?
c: No, because you cannot see it.
No, because it is not a solid.
Yes, because it has mass and takes up space.
items.e: You cannot see air, but it has mass and takes up space. A balloon gets bigger when you fill it with air.

items.q: What is matter?
c: anything that has mass and takes up space
items.e: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Air is matter even though you cannot see it.

items.q: Ice, liquid water and water vapor are made of
c: particles only when it is liquid
items.e: Ice, water and water vapor are all water. The particles are the same. Only how close they are and how they move changes.

items.q: A scientist says, “Everything around you is made of particles.” Which object is not included?
items.e: Light is energy, not matter, so it is not made of particles of matter.

items.q: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
items.e: A solid keeps its shape. A liquid takes the shape of its container, and a gas spreads out to fill it.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A shadow has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Air is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Steam and water vapor are which state of matter?
items.e: Water vapor is water as a gas. Its particles are far apart, so you cannot see it.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Salt has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: Heat has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. Carbon dioxide gas is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: Sunlight has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. A sugar cube is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Dust has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

items.q: Which of these is not matter?
items.e: A radio signal has no mass and does not take up space, so it is not matter. A pencil is matter: it is made of particles.

items.q: Which of these is matter?
items.e: Water has mass and takes up space, so it is matter. Light, heat, sound and shadows are not matter.

sets.title: Particle models of solids, liquids and gases

items.q: A model of a solid should show particles that are
c: touching but sliding at the bottom only
items.e: Solid particles are packed tightly in a pattern and vibrate in place.

items.q: In which state of matter do the particles stay in fixed places and only vibrate?
items.e: Solid particles are held in place. They vibrate but do not move past each other, so a solid keeps its shape.

items.q: Look at how close the particles are. Which state of matter is this?
items.e: In a gas the particles are far apart and move quickly in all directions.

items.q: Which state of matter can be squeezed into a much smaller space?
items.e: Gas particles have lots of space between them, so they can be pushed closer together.

items.q: Why is it hard to squeeze a block of wood into a smaller size?
c: Its particles are already packed close together.
Its particles are too big to move.
items.e: In a solid the particles are already touching, so there is almost no empty space to push them into.

items.q: Which is the same in an ice cube and in a puddle of the same water?
c: how close the particles are in a pattern
items.e: Both are made of water particles. The ice has them locked in place, and the puddle lets them slide.

items.q: The model shows the particles of a material at room temperature. Which material could it be?
items.e: The particles are touching but jumbled and free to slide past each other, so this is a liquid: water in a glass.

items.q: When water boils and turns into water vapor, the particles
c: move faster and spread far apart
items.e: Heating makes the particles move faster. In water vapor they are far apart, so you cannot see them.

items.q: When ice melts into water, what happens to the particles?
c: They stay the same but start to slide past each other.
items.e: Melting does not make new particles. The same water particles just move more freely.

items.q: What is between the particles of a gas?
items.e: There is empty space between gas particles. That is why gases can be compressed.

items.q: A student draws a model of air in a jar. Which drawing is best?
c: dots packed in neat rows at the bottom
a few dots spread out all over the jar
one big dot in the middle
items.e: Air is a gas, so the particles should be far apart and spread through the whole jar. An empty jar would mean air is nothing.

items.q: Why does a gas fill its whole container?
c: Its particles move freely and spread out.
items.e: Gas particles move quickly in every direction until they spread through the whole space. The particles themselves do not get bigger.

items.q: In which state of matter are the particles farthest apart?
c: They are the same distance apart in every state.
items.e: Gas particles are far apart. That is why a gas can be squeezed into a smaller space.

items.q: Why can a liquid be poured?
c: Its particles are very far apart.
Its particles can slide past each other.
Its particles do not move at all.
items.e: Liquid particles touch, but they are not locked in place. They slide past each other, so the liquid flows.

items.q: Look at how close the particles are. Which state of matter is this?
items.e: In a liquid the particles touch, but they are not in rows and they slide past each other.

items.q: The model shows the particles of a material at room temperature. Which material could it be?
items.e: The particles are packed in neat rows and touching, so this is a solid: a gold ring.

items.q: What state of matter is a material in, according to this model?
items.e: In a liquid the particles touch, but they are not in rows and they slide past each other.

items.q: The model shows the particles of a material at room temperature. Which material could it be?
items.e: The particles are packed in neat rows and touching, so this is a solid: a wooden block.

items.q: The model shows the particles of a material at room temperature. Which material could it be?
items.e: The particles are far apart and moving freely, so this is a gas: helium in a balloon.

items.q: Which state of matter does the model show?
items.e: In a solid the particles are packed tightly in a pattern and only vibrate in place.

items.q: A sealed syringe was filled with 60 mL of air. Then the plunger was pushed in to 30 mL. Nothing got out. What does this show?
c: The air particles were pushed closer together.
items.e: The same air particles are still inside. They now have less empty space between them, so they fit in 30 mL.

items.q: You pour 1 cup of sand into 1 cup of marbles and the total is less than 2 cups. How is this a model of mixing water and alcohol?
c: Small particles can fit into spaces between larger ones.
items.e: Particles of different sizes can fit into each other's gaps, just like sand fills the spaces between marbles.

items.q: Sugar is stirred into water and disappears. Which test would show that the sugar is still there?
c: Taste the water, or let it evaporate and look for sugar.
Put it in the freezer for 5 minutes.
Look at it with your eyes.
items.e: The water tastes sweet, and when it evaporates the sugar is left behind. The sugar was only too small to see.

items.q: Water drops form on the outside of a cold glass of lemonade. Where did the water come from?
c: lemonade that leaked through the glass
nowhere: it was made from nothing
water vapor in the air that cooled and turned into liquid
items.e: The air has water vapor in it. When the vapor touches the cold glass, its particles slow down and join into drops (condensation).

items.q: Which observation is evidence that air takes up space?
c: A cup pushed upside down into water stays dry inside.
items.e: The air trapped in the cup keeps the water out. Two things cannot take up the same space.

items.q: Ben pumps more air into a volleyball, and the ball gets firmer. What explains this?
c: The air in the ball turns into a solid.
The ball's rubber gets heavier by itself.
More air particles are packed inside the ball.
Air has no mass, so nothing changes.
items.e: Pumping adds more air particles. They push on the inside of the ball from all sides, so it feels firmer.

items.q: A puddle dries up on a sunny day. Where did the water go?
c: It soaked up into the clouds as a liquid at once.
It was destroyed by the sun.
Its particles went into the air as water vapor.
items.e: Water evaporates: its particles leave the puddle and move into the air as a gas, too small to see.

items.q: You can smell baking bread from 3 meters away, even though you cannot see anything moving through the air. What is the best explanation?
c: Smells are not made of anything.
The air in the room turns into the food.
The smell is light that travels to your eyes.
Tiny particles from it spread through the air to your nose.
items.e: Particles too small to see leave the source and spread out among the air particles until some reach your nose.

items.q: Food coloring spreads faster in hot water than in cold water. Why?
c: Particles move faster when they are warmer.
Coloring cannot mix with cold water.
items.e: Warmer particles move faster, so the coloring spreads out more quickly.

items.q: A person is spraying air freshener in one corner of a room. Soon people across the room can smell it. Which model explains this best?
c: The air freshener turning into heat
Waves of light moving across the room
Tiny particles moving and spreading through the air
The walls sending out the smell
items.e: The spray leaves tiny particles in the air. They keep moving and spread out across the room.

items.q: You stir salt into 200 mL of water until you cannot see it anymore. Where is it?
c: It broke into particles too small to see that are mixed in the water.
It is gone and no longer exists.
It sank and hid under the glass.
items.e: Dissolving breaks the salt into tiny particles that spread through the water. You can still taste it, and its mass is still there.

items.q: A balloon is put on the neck of an empty bottle. The bottle is placed in hot water and the balloon puffs up. Why?
c: The air particles move faster and spread out, pushing into the balloon.
The balloon gets heavier and bigger.
The water gets into the balloon.
New air is made by the hot water.
items.e: Heated air particles move faster and spread apart. They take up more space, so some move into the balloon.

items.q: A drop of food coloring is placed in still water. After an hour the whole glass is colored. What does this show?
c: Particles of coloring spread out among the water particles.
items.e: Particles of coloring and water are always moving. Over time the coloring particles spread through the water.

items.q: Omar dissolves 5 grams of salt in a dish of water. A week later all the water has evaporated. What is left in the dish?
items.e: The water particles went into the air, but the salt particles stayed. The same 5 grams of salt is left as crystals.

items.q: A sealed bag of chips puffs up when it is taken up a high mountain. What is inside the bag that causes this?
items.e: The bag is full of gas particles. With less air pushing on the bag from outside, the gas inside spreads out more.

items.q: A sealed syringe was filled with 50 mL of air. Then the plunger was pushed in to 20 mL. Nothing got out. What does this show?
c: The air particles were pushed closer together.
items.e: The same air particles are still inside. They now have less empty space between them, so they fit in 20 mL.

items.q: Nora pumps more air into a soccer ball, and the ball gets firmer. What explains this?
c: The air in the ball turns into a solid.
Air has no mass, so nothing changes.
The ball's rubber gets heavier by itself.
More air particles are packed inside the ball.
items.e: Pumping adds more air particles. They push on the inside of the ball from all sides, so it feels firmer.

items.q: You can smell an orange being peeled from 3 meters away, even though you cannot see anything moving through the air. What is the best explanation?
c: Tiny particles from it spread through the air to your nose.
Smells are not made of anything.
The smell is light that travels to your eyes.
The air in the room turns into the food.
items.e: Particles too small to see leave the source and spread out among the air particles until some reach your nose.

items.q: You stir salt into 100 mL of water until you cannot see it anymore. Where is it?
c: It is gone and no longer exists.
It broke into particles too small to see that are mixed in the water.
It sank and hid under the glass.
items.e: Dissolving breaks the salt into tiny particles that spread through the water. You can still taste it, and its mass is still there.

items.q: Eli dissolves 15 grams of salt in a dish of water. A week later all the water has evaporated. What is left in the dish?
items.e: The water particles went into the air, but the salt particles stayed. The same 15 grams of salt is left as crystals.

items.q: Two identical sealed jars are on a balance. One is filled with air pumped in tightly, the other has normal air. Which side goes down?
c: the jar with extra air pumped in
items.e: More air particles means more mass, so that side of the balance goes down.

items.q: Why does a ball filled with air have more mass than the same ball when it is flat?
c: Rubber gets heavier when it stretches.
It does not: air has no mass.
items.e: Each air particle has a tiny mass. Many of them together add up to a mass you can measure.

items.q: An empty scuba tank has a mass of 15 kg. Filled with air pressed in tightly, it has a mass of 18 kg. Which conclusion is correct?
c: The air inside has a mass of 3 kg.
The air inside has a mass of 18 kg.
The tank itself gained 3 kg of metal.
items.e: 18 − 15 = 3 kg of air. Packing more air particles into the tank adds mass.

items.q: Salt water is boiled until all the water is gone. A white solid is left. What is the solid?
c: the salt that was dissolved in the water
items.e: The salt was in the water the whole time as tiny particles. Only the water left as vapor.

items.q: Which units are used to measure mass in science class?
items.e: Mass is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). Liters measure volume.

items.q: A balloon holds 2 liters of air. All of the air is pumped into a box that holds only 1 liter, and the box is sealed. What is in the box?
c: only 1 liter's worth of particles, the rest disappeared
all the same air particles, pushed closer together
items.e: A gas can be compressed. The particles move closer together, but none of them disappear.

items.q: 30 g of sugar is stirred into 250 g of water until it disappears. What is the mass of the sugar water?
items.e: The sugar is still there as tiny particles: 250 + 30 = 280 g.

items.q: A flat beach ball has a mass of 475 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 490 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 490 − 475 = 15 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: Which tool is used to measure the mass of a sample of matter?
items.e: Mass is measured with a balance or a scale, in grams or kilograms.

items.q: A dish of salt water has a mass of 150 g (not counting the dish). It contains 20 g of salt. After all the water evaporates, what is the mass of what is left in the dish?
items.e: Only the water evaporated. The 20 g of salt stays behind. The other 130 g of water went into the air as vapor.

items.q: A cup of water is placed on a scale. Sugar is dissolved in it. What happens to the reading on the scale?
c: It stays the same because sugar disappears.
It goes back to the mass of the water.
It goes up by the mass of the sugar.
items.e: The sugar is still in the cup as tiny particles, so its mass is added.

items.q: An empty scuba tank has a mass of 10 kg. Filled with air pressed in tightly, it has a mass of 12 kg. Which conclusion is correct?
c: The tank itself gained 2 kg of metal.
The air inside has a mass of 12 kg.
The air inside has a mass of 2 kg.
items.e: 12 − 10 = 2 kg of air. Packing more air particles into the tank adds mass.

items.q: 40 g of sugar is stirred into 150 g of water until it disappears. What is the mass of the sugar water?
items.e: The sugar is still there as tiny particles: 150 + 40 = 190 g.

items.q: A flat soccer ball has a mass of 534 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 552 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 552 − 534 = 18 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: A dish of salt water has a mass of 150 g (not counting the dish). It contains 40 g of salt. After all the water evaporates, what is the mass of what is left in the dish?
items.e: Only the water evaporated. The 40 g of salt stays behind. The other 110 g of water went into the air as vapor.

items.q: An empty scuba tank has a mass of 13 kg. Filled with air pressed in tightly, it has a mass of 19 kg. Which conclusion is correct?
c: The air inside has a mass of 19 kg.
The air inside has a mass of 6 kg.
The tank itself gained 6 kg of metal.
items.e: 19 − 13 = 6 kg of air. Packing more air particles into the tank adds mass.

items.q: 20 g of salt is stirred into 100 g of water until it disappears. What is the mass of the salt water?
items.e: The salt is still there as tiny particles: 100 + 20 = 120 g.

items.q: A flat ball has a mass of 500 g. After it is pumped full of air, its mass is 519 g. What is the mass of the air inside?
items.e: 519 − 500 = 19 g. The air added mass, so air is matter.

items.q: A dish of salt water has a mass of 260 g (not counting the dish). It contains 10 g of salt. After all the water evaporates, what is the mass of what is left in the dish?
items.e: Only the water evaporated. The 10 g of salt stays behind. The other 250 g of water went into the air as vapor.

items.q: An empty scuba tank has a mass of 13 kg. Filled with air pressed in tightly, it has a mass of 18 kg. Which conclusion is correct?
c: The air inside has a mass of 5 kg.
The air inside has a mass of 18 kg.
The tank itself gained 5 kg of metal.
items.e: 18 − 13 = 5 kg of air. Packing more air particles into the tank adds mass.

items.q: Maya puts a balloon on the neck of a bottle and moves the bottle from hot water into ice water. What happens to the balloon?
c: It shrinks, because the air particles slow down and move closer together.
items.e: Cooling slows the particles, so the air takes up less space and the balloon goes flat.

items.q: Ravi seals the tip of a syringe filled with sand and pushes the plunger. What should he observe?
c: The syringe gets lighter as you push.
The plunger moves in easily, because air particles have space between them.
The plunger hardly moves, because the grains and their particles are already packed.
The plunger hardly moves, because water particles are already close together.
items.e: Only a gas can be squeezed much. Liquids and solids already have their particles close together.

items.q: Which question could be answered with a particle model?
c: Why does a gas spread to fill a room?
items.e: A particle model explains how matter behaves, like gas particles moving and spreading out.

items.q: A student says that a jar with only air in it is empty. Which experiment shows the jar is not empty?
c: Push the upside-down jar into water: water does not fill it.
Weigh the jar on a bathroom scale.
items.e: Air inside the jar takes up space, so water cannot get in. A bathroom scale is not exact enough to show the air's tiny mass.

items.q: Noah wraps an ice cube in a bag, seals it and weighs it: 25 g. He weighs it again after it melts. What should the scale show?
items.e: Melting does not add or remove particles. The water has the same mass as the ice: 25 g.

items.q: Leo says that when sugar dissolves, it is destroyed. Which evidence best shows he is wrong?
c: The mass of the water plus sugar stays the same before and after stirring.
items.e: If the sugar were destroyed, the mass would go down. It stays the same, so the sugar is still there as tiny particles.

items.q: Students put the same amount of food coloring in hot water and in cold water. What should they keep the same to make it a fair test?
c: the color only in one cup
the amount of water and the size of the cups
items.e: Only the temperature should be different. Everything else, like the amount of water and coloring, should stay the same.

items.q: Ava wants to show that air has mass. Which investigation is best?
c: Look at air with a hand lens.
Measure the temperature of the air.
Weigh a flat ball, pump it up, then weigh it again.
Blow on her hand and feel it.
items.e: Comparing the mass before and after adding air shows that the air itself has mass.

items.q: A class leaves two dishes of salt water in the sun. One dish is covered with plastic wrap. After 3 days, which dish has dry salt crystals?
items.e: In the open dish the water vapor escapes into the air. Under the wrap the vapor is trapped and drips back down.

items.q: Omar notices that a bicycle tire looks a little flat on a cold morning and fuller on a hot afternoon. No air was added. Why?
c: The tire made more air during the day.
Warm air particles move faster and push harder on the tire.
items.e: The same air is inside. When it warms, the particles move faster and push outward more.

items.q: Which statement best describes a good model of matter?
c: It shows tiny particles that are always moving.
It shows only things you can see.
It shows matter as one solid piece with no parts.
It shows particles that never move.
items.e: Scientists model all matter as tiny particles in motion. The spacing and motion depend on the state of matter.

The plunger moves in easily, because air particles have space between them.
The plunger hardly moves, because the grains and their particles are already packed.
